definition: A force of attraction that holds atoms or ions together in a compound.
A strong electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions. Formed when a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal.
A bond formed when two atoms share a pair of electrons. Found in non-metal elements and compounds.
The electrostatic attraction between a lattice of positive metal ions and a sea of delocalised electrons.
A charged particle formed when an atom gains or loses electrons. Metal atoms lose electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions.
The process by which electrons move from one atom to another during the formation of an ionic bond.
A diagram used to show the arrangement of outer shell electrons in atoms and how they are shared or transferred during bonding.
A giant, regular three-dimensional arrangement of oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
A compound formed from positive and negative ions arranged in a giant ionic lattice. Has high melting and boiling points.
The force of attraction between oppositely charged particles (e.g. positive and negative ions in an ionic lattice).
A molecule made of a small number of atoms joined by covalent bonds. Has low melting and boiling points because intermolecular forces are weak.
A substance in which a very large number of atoms are joined by covalent bonds in a regular lattice. Has very high melting points. Examples include diamond and silicon dioxide.
A form of carbon in which each carbon atom is covalently bonded to four others in a giant lattice. Very hard with a very high melting point. Does not conduct electricity.
A form of carbon in which each atom is bonded to three others in layers. The layers can slide over each other making it soft and slippery. Has delocalised electrons so conducts electricity.
A single layer of graphite — one atom thick — with a hexagonal arrangement of carbon atoms. Very strong, lightweight, and an excellent conductor of electricity.
A molecule of carbon atoms arranged in hollow spheres, tubes, or other shapes. Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) is a well-known example. Used in drug delivery and nanotechnology.
A cylindrical fullerene made of carbon atoms. Has a very high tensile strength and conducts electricity. Used in electronics and as a catalyst.
A weak force of attraction between molecules. These forces determine the melting and boiling points of simple molecular substances.
An electron that is not associated with a single atom or bond but is free to move throughout a structure. Responsible for electrical conductivity in metals and graphite.
A giant structure of positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons. The strong electrostatic attraction gives metals their characteristic properties.
A mixture of a metal with one or more other elements (usually metals or carbon). Alloys are often harder and stronger than pure metals because the different-sized atoms disrupt the regular lattice.
The ability of a metal to be hammered or rolled into shape without breaking, due to layers of ions being able to slide over each other.
The ability to transfer heat or electricity. Metals are good conductors because their delocalised electrons can move freely and carry charge or energy.
A large molecule made up of many small repeating units (monomers) joined together in a long chain by covalent bonds.
A small molecule that can join with many others to form a polymer.
A giant covalent structure in which each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms. Has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.
One of the three physical forms a substance can take: solid, liquid, or gas. Determined by the strength of forces between particles and temperature.
The temperature at which a solid changes into a liquid. Substances with stronger bonds or forces between particles have higher melting points.
The temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas. Related to the strength of intermolecular forces in simple molecular substances.
A particle between 1 and 100 nanometres in size. Has a very large surface area to volume ratio, giving it different properties to the bulk material.
A unit of length equal to one billionth of a metre (1 × 10⁻⁹ m). Used to measure the size of nanoparticles and atoms.
